source.title: The wild west of bodybuilding supplements: Three examples of unregulated compounds widely marketed online

paper.citation: Dhaliwal R., Pope H.G. The wild west of bodybuilding supplements: Three examples of unregulated compounds widely marketed online. Performance Enhancement & Health. 2026;14(3):100424. doi:10.1016/j.peh.2026.100424.
paper.abstract: This paper addresses the following question: How large is online interest in three representative bodybuilding compounds, how much human and safety research exists, how familiar are sports-medicine authors with them, and how accurately do selected turkesterone products match their labels? The study did not enroll athletes as an intervention cohort. It analyzed worldwide internet activity and product listings, reviewed PubMed literature, surveyed corresponding authors of papers indexed under “sports medicine,” and chemically analyzed ten turkesterone products bought online. The authors combined Google Trends data from 2022 through 2024, accessible Bodybuilding.com and Reddit discussions, YouTube videos, online seller listings, and Amazon review or purchase proxies. PubMed searches counted human, anabolic-effect, and safety papers.
paper.tldr: Relative Google search interest for turkesterone, ibutamoren, and ostarine was 2.39, 1.42, and 1.96 times the interest in nandrolone, respectively, within the authors’ specified comparison. Online forums, videos, and sellers showed extensive discussion and ready availability, including content apparently aimed at or used by teenagers; these engagement metrics indicate visibility, not verified prevalence or safe use. Ask nonjudgmentally and specifically about SARMs, “research chemicals,” growth-hormone secretagogues, ecdysteroids, stacks, and products promoted by influencers—not only conventional vitamins or anabolic steroids.
paper.methods: The authors combined Google Trends data from 2022 through 2024, accessible Bodybuilding.com and Reddit discussions, YouTube videos, online seller listings, and Amazon review or purchase proxies. PubMed searches counted human, anabolic-effect, and safety papers. An anonymous familiarity survey was sent to 6,885 email addresses scraped from sports-medicine publications, and ten products advertised as turkesterone underwent liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry.
paper.findings: Relative Google search interest for turkesterone, ibutamoren, and ostarine was 2.39, 1.42, and 1.96 times the interest in nandrolone, respectively, within the authors’ specified comparison. Online forums, videos, and sellers showed extensive discussion and ready availability, including content apparently aimed at or used by teenagers; these engagement metrics indicate visibility, not verified prevalence or safe use. The PubMed review found only two human turkesterone studies and no systematic human safety study; results on anabolic effects were conflicting. Ibutamoren evidence was concentrated in older or growth-hormone-deficient populations, included adverse effects, and did not establish performance benefits in healthy athletes; growth-hormone secretagogues are prohibited in sport. Ostarine had limited human research and case reports of serious adverse events; as a SARM, it is prohibited in sport and is not an approved dietary supplement. None of ten products advertised as turkesterone contained more than 0.5% of the labeled amount, and other unlabeled ecdysteroids were detected; the analysis did not comprehensively identify all possible adulterants. Only 375 of roughly 6,500 delivered professional surveys were returned, and respondents showed very low familiarity with the three target compounds.
paper.limitations: Digital-search, post, view, upvote, review, and purchase-proxy metrics cannot identify unique users, confirm ingestion, establish demographics, or produce prevalence estimates. Search-term choices and inaccessible posts can undercount or bias comparisons, while publicity can inflate interest. The professional survey had a response rate below 6%, a heterogeneous sampling frame, and substantial selection-bias risk. The PubMed analysis was bibliometric rather than a formal systematic review with risk-of-bias grading. Only ten turkesterone products were chemically tested, so the results do not estimate the entire market or prove the contents of any other product. Applicability to collegiate American football is practical rather than population-specific: athletes may encounter these products online, but the study did not measure football-player use or outcomes.
paper.practicalImplications: Ask nonjudgmentally and specifically about SARMs, “research chemicals,” growth-hormone secretagogues, ecdysteroids, stacks, and products promoted by influencers—not only conventional vitamins or anabolic steroids. Treat ostarine and ibutamoren as prohibited/high-risk athlete-health and anti-doping concerns, and do not infer safety from “natural,” “research use only,” or dietary-supplement labeling. A third-party certification lowers but does not eliminate risk; products from unregulated online sources should not be used. When exposure is disclosed, involve sports medicine, sports dietetics, and compliance, document the exact product and lot if available, and consult the current governing-body and WADA rules.

paper.rtp: The paper did not validate a rehabilitation or return-to-sport decision rule. Its findings may inform supporting training or monitoring during reconditioning, but it provides no standalone clearance threshold or progression criterion.
